The proposed method is supported by theoretical analysis and experimental validation. The results show that our approach significantly reduces communication costs while maintaining comparable performance. In modern society, multilingual individuals frequently switch between languages
in spoken and written communication. This code-mixing phenomenon is particularly
common among multilingual populations, who often combine elements from different
languages to convey complex ideas or emotions. Despite its prevalence, code-

Language Processing. This paper aims to address this knowledge gap by examining
the complexities and constraints surrounding code-mixing in NLP applications
within diverse linguistic environments. We also highlight key factors influencing
code-mixing and suggest potential avenues for future research and development.

In the realm of online advertising, predicting click-through rates is a critical task, 
with current models primarily focusing on the interplay between user interests and 
advertisements. However, this approach overlooks the significance of visual content 
within advertisements. To address this, we propose a novel framework that leverages 
multimodal learning to incorporate visual elements into the prediction process. 
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding a 1.04% 
absolute improvement in CTR prediction accuracy. Furthermore, our model's ability 
to generalize is highlighted by its ability to accurately forecast CTRs for new 
advertisements. The source code for this paper is publicly available on GitHub at 
https://github.com/zhaozheng1997/VisualEnhance.

Organizational operations are often governed by established procedures,

adherence. This research focuses on a specific type of monitoring, known as 
prescriptive procedure monitoring, where the system is aware of the 
underlying process definition and can identify deviations from the expected 
protocol. This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of this type 
of monitoring by examining its core aspects, including the underlying 
challenges, applicable methods, and relevant evaluation metrics. Ultimately, 
the findings are intended to inform future research in this area.

The model's success also sheds light on the challenges of measuring shear thickening rates and the importance of considering particle alignment in interpreting experimental results. Deep neural networks tend to develop straightforward solutions to complex problems, 
and our research reveals that the architecture itself is the primary factor behind this phenomenon. 
We demonstrate that the numerous layers within a neural network effectively limit its solution options, 
resulting in the discovery of simpler models. 
To support this finding, we developed a mathematical framework that measures the constraints imposed by a network's architecture, 
and our experiments using various network configurations and problem types confirm the validity of this theory. 
Ultimately, our research suggests that the architecture of a neural network can be optimized to yield more accurate predictions. 
We also show that the architecture's influence on solution complexity can be leveraged to develop more efficient neural network models. 
Our findings are documented in detail in the paper titled "Why neural networks discover simple solutions: the many regularizers of geometric complexity."

We analyze the behavior of the standard estimators for the parameters of a Cauchy distribution, considering both maximum likelihood and a modified method that uses the sample median. Our study focuses on the asymptotic behavior of these estimators, particularly how they behave as sample sizes increase, and we also examine their finite sample properties. Our findings reveal that the traditional approach yields estimators with non-deterministic convergence and infinite variance, whereas the alternative method produces estimators with deterministic convergence and finite variance. Building on this, we establish the asymptotic distribution of the estimators and propose a method for constructing confidence intervals and squares. Our results are substantiated through simulations and a real-data example. Additionally, we discuss the applicability of our findings to other distributions with similar characteristics. The associated R code is provided for reference. 

Keywords: Asymptotic behavior, Cauchy distribution, Confidence intervals, Finite sample properties, Median-based estimation.

In the realm of fashion, visual compatibility plays a crucial role in creating stylish and cohesive outfits. However, the complexity of this task lies in its multi-faceted nature, requiring not only visual but also semantic understanding of the input. To address this challenge, we introduce VICTOR, a novel approach that leverages a combination of transformer-based encoders and a custom-built, fashion-centric pre-training framework. By pre-training on a vast, user-generated dataset, VICTOR learns to capture the inherent visual characteristics of fashion items, enabling it to excel in identifying incompatible outfit configurations. Our experiments demonstrate VICTOR's superiority over state-of-the-art models, with a notable improvement of 10.4% in accuracy on the Fashion-Incompatibility dataset. Furthermore, VICTOR's ability to generalize across domains is showcased through its successful application on the Outfit2Vec dataset. We develop a framework for creating high-dimensional extensions of set cover instances, yielding two general methods for achieving this. These methods are founded on two distinct concepts: the first involves the idea of near-uniqueness in set cover instances, while the second centers on the notion of a specific type of structure within hypergraphs. By applying these ideas, we are able to derive two new high-dimensional extension methods. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of obtaining high-dimensional extensions within the context of a specific class of set cover instances, ultimately identifying a key constraint that hinders such instances from supporting high-dimensional extensions. This constraint is subsequently shown to be a necessary condition as well. Our work also explores the relationship between high-dimensional extensions and a concept known as the 'Shelah number' in the context of set theory. Additionally, we present a new upper bound on the 'Shelah number' for the specific class of set cover instances, offering a simplified explanation of the underlying reasoning. The power graph of a group G, denoted as $\Gamma(G)$, is a graph that consists of G's elements as vertices and has a directed edge from one element to another if the latter's order is a multiple of the former. In this research, we establish the minimum order of finite nilpotent groups based on their power graphs. Specifically, we demonstrate that there are two classes of groups: those whose order is a perfect power of two and others whose order is a perfect power of a prime number. Additionally, we show that for a given prime number, there exists a group of the lowest possible order in each class, and that class-specific group orders are infinite in number. Furthermore, we provide a general formula for the minimum order of power nilpotent groups of a given prime number. Lastly, we present a question regarding the existence of groups with a specific order. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) rely on spatially translation-invariant features, 
which are derived from local patterns within images. However, this assumption 
breaks down when dealing with global image characteristics. To address this, we 
propose a new type of convolutional layer that can capture direction-dependent 
patterns in images. This is achieved through a novel weight structure that 
efficiently enables the extraction of features from any orientation. As a result, 
our direction convolutional networks (DCNs) can learn more comprehensive and 
robust representations, leading to improved performance in various image 
recognition tasks. Furthermore, our DCNs can be seamlessly integrated into 
existing CNN architectures, allowing for a straightforward adaptation to a range 
of applications. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of DCNs in achieving 
state-of-the-art results for image classification, object detection, and 
segmentation. The code for our approach is available at the link provided.

We introduce a new data structure, the XOR filter, which outperforms Bloom filters and Cuckoo filters in terms of memory usage and processing speed. The XOR filter's efficiency stems from its ability to utilize a smaller amount of memory and the fact that lookup operations can be performed in constant time. Our research involves comparing the characteristics of XOR filters with those of Bloom and Cuckoo filters, including an in-depth analysis of the former's behavior. Additionally, we present a method for optimizing the performance of XOR filters, which involves selecting the most suitable parameters based on the desired trade-off between memory usage and processing speed. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations, which demonstrate the advantages of XOR filters over Bloom and Cuckoo filters in various scenarios. Specifically, XOR filters offer improved performance in applications where a moderate number of false positives is acceptable and memory usage needs to be minimized. On the other hand, Bloom filters are more suitable for scenarios where a low error rate is required, while Cuckoo filters offer improved performance in applications with a very high number of elements. Ultimately, our research provides a framework for selecting the most appropriate filter type based on the specific requirements of each use case. In multi-task reinforcement learning, the issue of catastrophic interference arises when previously learned information is destroyed during new task acquisition. Our research focuses on a specific type of interference known as overwriting, which occurs when a new task's experiences replace the agent's prior experiences. We introduce a modular architecture for agents that learns policies and value functions, allowing each task to be stored in a separate network. This approach prevents overwriting and enables the agent to retain learned skills across various tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that agents with this modular architecture can successfully acquire multiple skills without interference, and we also show that this design can be applied to a range of existing multi-task reinforcement learning methods to prevent catastrophic interference. Furthermore, we found that the agent's ability to learn from short-term experience is crucial in overcoming the interference challenge. Our research provides a foundation for developing more sophisticated methods to address catastrophic interference in reinforcement learning. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, which builds upon the WaveNet architecture to capture the intricate patterns in speech and audio signals. By incorporating a pitch-dependent expansion factor into the dilated convolution operation, Quasi-Periodic WaveNet effectively models signals with varying periods of correlation. Through experiments, we demonstrate that our model outperforms the conventional WaveNet architecture in terms of sample efficiency and generated signal quality. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the model's ability to model signals of different periods is a key factor in its improved performance. Our model source code will be made publicly available.

biclustering to enhance user preference prediction. Biclustering enables the
identification of overlapping user groups sharing similar rating patterns in
multiple subspaces within the item rating matrix. We propose a method to
automatically determine the size of these user groups based on the principle
of minimal information gain. Experimental results on real-world datasets reveal
the effectiveness of our approach in outperforming state-of-the-art models.

user preferences by incorporating a sparsity penalty and utilizing the mean
absolute error as a subjective preference regularization term.
